quoted_clause: The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the server tier as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts at the 40 rps peak
observed: Table 13-1 defines 'Server' as one host with 1–8 GPUs and 'Cluster' as multiple hosts (tens to hundreds of GPUs). A fleet of ~21 hosts is a cluster by that definition. The sentence tries to distinguish 'server-class model residency' from 'cluster-tier deployment,' but it uses 'server tier' for the deployment, which contradicts the table.
evidence: The same paragraph later says 'the traffic scaling is a cluster of server-class hosts, not weight-splitting' and 'the server tier is the right model-residency archetype ... It does not mean one host serves the whole arrival rate.' The intended distinction is clear, but the first sentence's tier label is wrong.
root_cause: The chapter uses 'tier' both for model-residency class and for deployment scale without disambiguating the two.
correction: Rewrite the first sentence as: 'The canonical workload's model residency is server-class, but its deployment at the 40 rps peak is a cluster of ~21 server-class hosts.' Then use 'server-class residency' and 'cluster-tier deployment' consistently in §13.3 and §13.6.
acceptance_test: The tier label in §13.3 matches Table 13-1's definition: one host = Server; multiple hosts = Cluster. A reader cannot conclude that a 21-host fleet is a single server-tier deployment.

quoted_clause: each per-layer all-reduce is ~0.45 MB sent per rank — batch × hidden × bytes, sub-MB to a few MB
observed: The parenthetical formula 'batch × hidden × bytes' gives the logical input tensor size, not the bytes sent per rank by a ring all-reduce. For a ring, each rank sends 2(N−1)/N times the logical tensor across reduce-scatter plus all-gather, or 1.75× for N=8. With batch 16, hidden 8,192, and BF16, the logical input is 256 KiB; the ring send per rank is 448 KiB. The quoted '~0.45 MB sent per rank' is consistent with the ring send, but the formula beside it is not.
evidence: The chapter's own §10.3 calculation uses M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 256 KiB and then 1.75M = 448 KiB sent per rank. The mini-case's parenthetical omits the 1.75 factor.
root_cause: The text mixes logical tensor size with physical ring send volume in one parenthetical.
correction: Change to: 'each per-layer all-reduce has a logical input of batch × hidden × bytes; the ring send per rank is 1.75× that for an eight-rank ring, about 0.45 MB in this example.'
acceptance_test: Recomputing from the quoted formula yields the quoted sent-per-rank number, including the ring normalization.

quoted_clause: up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget
observed: Section 12.3 defines the canonical per-host budget as 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB. The §12.8 parenthetical gives 140 + 436 = 576 GB and calls it 'up to ~576 GB' without the ~64 GB runtime term. That is a partial sum, not the full host residency. A reader can misread 576 GB as the total residency and conclude there is 64 GB of headroom when the text elsewhere says zero headroom.
evidence: Section 12.3: '140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom.' Section 12.8: 'up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget.' The arithmetic is internally inconsistent in labeling.
root_cause: The §12.8 summary drops the runtime term that §12.3 includes.
correction: Write 'up to ~576 GB of weights+KV, plus ~64 GB runtime, for ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget' or simply 'up to ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget.'
acceptance_test: The candidate (b) residency arithmetic in §12.8 sums to the same total and headroom as §12.3.

quoted_clause: The analytical KV quotient C ≈ 17.5 FP16-KV request-equivalents (436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token request; 9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB) gives at most 17 whole-context slots, not a deployable concurrency of 17.5.
observed: The arithmetic is correct, but the text uses 9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output) as the per-request KV footprint while the canonical workload is described as ~9,200 input tokens. The 9,500-token figure is a maximum sequence length, not the request's input length. This is defensible as a conservative whole-context slot calculation, but the prose does not state that the 9,500 includes the 300 output tokens and therefore may confuse readers who expect the KV quotient to be based on input tokens alone.
evidence: 9,500 × 2.62 MB = 24,890 MB = 24.89 GB; 436 / 24.9 = 17.51. The calculation is internally consistent. The issue is explanatory: the text should explicitly say '9,500-token maximum sequence (9,200 input + 300 output)' so the reader does not think the canonical input is 9,500 tokens.
root_cause: The canonical workload's input and output token counts are combined for KV sizing without a local reminder of the decomposition.
correction: Rewrite the parenthetical as: '(436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token maximum sequence; 9,500 = 9,200 input + 300 output; 9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB)'.
acceptance_test: A reader can state why the KV quotient uses 9,500 tokens even though the canonical input is 9,200 tokens, and can reproduce 436 / 24.9 ≈ 17.5.

quoted_clause: TPOT p50/p95 (≤ ~25 ms median).
observed: The bullet says 'p50/p95' but then gives only a median bound. A p95 TPOT bound is not stated, so the reader cannot tell whether the p95 value is merely recorded or also constrained. This is a small but real ambiguity in a chapter about precise benchmark contracts.
evidence: The canonical SLO elsewhere is 'TPOT ~25 ms/token' and the worksheet row says '~25 ms/token median'. The bullet's parenthetical should match that scope or state both bounds.
root_cause: The bullet conflates the metric list (p50/p95) with the SLO bound (median only).
correction: Change to: 'TPOT p50/p95 (SLO: p50 ≤ ~25 ms/token; record p95 for tail diagnosis).'
acceptance_test: The benchmark protocol unambiguously states which TPOT percentiles are SLO-bound and which are diagnostic.

quoted_clause: The "4 chars ≈ 1 token" estimate can be ~1.5–3× off for code/JSON/technical text (measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer).
observed: The 1.5–3× range is plausible but unsourced and unlabeled. In a chapter that insists on evidence labels and measured values, this empirical claim should carry a scope or be softened. It is not clear whether the range is measured, illustrative, or rule-of-thumb.
evidence: The sentence gives no citation, no measurement context, and no evidence label. The chapter elsewhere is careful to label illustrative and derived claims.
root_cause: A useful heuristic is stated with more quantitative precision than the surrounding evidence standard supports.
correction: Either add a source/measurement note, or rewrite as: 'The 4-chars-per-token heuristic can be materially wrong for code/JSON/technical text; measure chars/token with the model's own tokenizer rather than assuming a fixed ratio.' If the 1.5–3× range is retained, label it [ILLUSTRATIVE] or cite a measurement.
acceptance_test: The claim's evidence status is explicit, and a reader knows whether 1.5–3× is a measured range or an illustrative heuristic.

page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Measure drafts, commitments and valid results separately'
quoted_clause: Those are different events. A first-draft timestamp measures early visibility. A first-commit timestamp measures when a downstream consumer can safely act on text that will not be overwritten. Time to a validated answer includes any required schema checks, unit tests or task acceptance. Comparisons need the same boundary on both sides. [1P][FACT]; metric definitions [DERIVED]
observed: The [1P][FACT] label is applied to a conceptual distinction, not a first-party measurement or specification. The distinction is sound, but labeling it [1P][FACT] overstates provenance. It is a derived metric-definition argument, not a first-party fact.
evidence: The sentence defines draft/commit/validated-answer boundaries. No first-party source is cited. The adjacent clause already says 'metric definitions [DERIVED]', which conflicts with the [1P][FACT] label on the same span.
root_cause: Evidence-label scope is too broad: the [1P][FACT] label binds the whole clause rather than only the uncontroversial observation that these are different events.
correction: Change the label to '[DERIVED]' for the metric-definition span, or split the sentence: the observation that services can expose drafts and commits may be [1P][FACT] if a first-party source exists; the metric-boundary recommendation is [DERIVED].
acceptance_test: The label matches the provenance of the claim: no first-party fact is asserted without a first-party source.

quoted_clause: Two-stage benchmarking: the capability screen (which models qualify) feeds the deployment benchmark (which system meets our SLO), whose results pass the TCO + SLO gate to the deployed system, feeding selection and TCO.
observed: The caption's causal order is muddled: deployment benchmark results 'pass the TCO + SLO gate to the deployed system, feeding selection and TCO.' Selection should precede deployment, and TCO should follow selection/deployment measurement. The phrase 'feeding selection and TCO' after 'deployed system' makes the diagram's reading order ambiguous.
evidence: The chapter's own §6 bullet list gives the correct order: capability screen → deployment benchmark → chosen system → TCO and performance engineering. The caption should match that order.
root_cause: The caption compresses the two-stage flow and the downstream TCO gate into one sentence, losing the sequence.
correction: Rewrite the caption to: 'Two-stage benchmarking: the capability screen selects qualifying models; the deployment benchmark measures each survivor on the canonical workload; the resulting SLO-goodput and cost feed selection and TCO.'
acceptance_test: A reader can infer the correct sequence from the caption alone: screen → benchmark → select → TCO.

quoted_clause: Suppose candidate A (70B dense on 8×H100) passes the capability screen and achieves p95 TTFT 1.9 s at an illustrative offered load of 1.3 req/s, with the other request SLOs also satisfied.
observed: The example says 'with the other request SLOs also satisfied' but the canonical SLO includes median TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s, and TPOT ~25 ms. The text gives only p95 TTFT 1.9 s. It does not state the median TTFT or TPOT values, so 'other request SLOs also satisfied' is asserted rather than shown. This is acceptable for an illustrative example, but the chapter's standard is to make the acceptance boundary explicit.
evidence: The example is labeled [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED], so it is not a factual claim. The issue is pedagogical: the reader cannot see which SLO rows are satisfied.
root_cause: The illustrative result compresses several SLO checks into one phrase.
correction: Add a short parenthetical: '(e.g., median TTFT 1.1 s, TPOT p50 24 ms; all within the stated SLOs)' or explicitly say 'the example assumes the unstated SLO rows are satisfied.'
acceptance_test: The reader can distinguish which SLO values are illustrated and which are merely assumed.

page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'A video benchmark is a workload tuple'
quoted_clause: HunyuanVideo-1.5 reports 5.5070 versus 2.9475 seconds per diffusion step for dense versus sparse attention at 720 × 1,280 pixels and 241 frames. Those measurements use eight H800 GPUs with context parallelism and a CFG-distilled model. Its separate 50-step table adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching, and reports 96.78 versus 58.39 seconds for the same shape.
observed: The phrase 'for the same shape' is potentially misleading: the 50-step table adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching, so it is not the same experimental configuration as the per-step table. 'Same shape' appears to mean same pixel dimensions and frame count, not same recipe. The text should say 'same pixel/frame shape' to avoid implying identical settings.
evidence: The preceding sentence explicitly says the 50-step table 'adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching.' That is a different configuration.
root_cause: Shorthand 'same shape' conflates spatial/temporal shape with experimental recipe.
correction: Change 'for the same shape' to 'for the same pixel/frame shape but with the added optimizations listed above.'
acceptance_test: A reader cannot mistake the 50-step table for a controlled comparison against the per-step table.

page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Two fair comparisons answer different questions'
quoted_clause: A p95 threshold is a configuration-level statistic; it is not itself a count of compliant work.
observed: This is correct but potentially confusing in context. The paragraph is about request goodput and token goodput. Saying a p95 threshold is 'configuration-level' is true, but the reader may wonder how a p95 SLO is enforced per request. The text should clarify that a p95 SLO is evaluated over a population/window, while goodput counts requests that individually satisfy their SLOs.
evidence: The surrounding text distinguishes request goodput from token goodput but does not explicitly connect percentile SLO evaluation to per-request compliance.
root_cause: The sentence states a statistical fact without linking it to the goodput definition.
correction: Add: 'A p95 SLO is evaluated over a defined population and window; goodput then counts the requests that individually meet their SLOs within that window.'
acceptance_test: The reader can explain how a p95 SLO and request goodput coexist without contradiction.

quoted_clause: Mean-only latency reporting. A 0.84 s mean hides a 5 s tail that breaches the p95 SLO (Ch6).
observed: The 0.84 s mean and 5 s tail are presented without an evidence label or source. In a chapter that is otherwise careful about labeling illustrative numbers, this reads as a measured example. It may be canonical, but the local text does not say so.
evidence: No citation or label appears. The number may be from Ch6, but the reader of Ch14 cannot tell.
root_cause: A cross-chapter example is reused without a local label or reference.
correction: Add '[CANONICAL]' or 'e.g., in the Ch6 example' so the number's status is clear.
acceptance_test: The reader knows whether 0.84 s / 5 s is a measured, canonical, or illustrative pair.

page_hint: Chapter 14 §4 'Acceptance test for a quantized deployment'
quoted_clause: A bounded first screen can use at least 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point, but these are illustrative starting budgets, not proof of rare-failure or p99 reliability.
observed: The phrase 'at least 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point' is labeled illustrative, which is good. However, 'three repetitions per load point' is very weak for tail-latency or p99 claims, and the text says so. The issue is that the sentence may still be read as a recommended minimum. It should explicitly say this is a smoke-screen, not a p99-valid experiment.
evidence: The sentence already says 'not proof of rare-failure or p99 reliability.' The recommendation is therefore adequately qualified. This is a minor clarity issue, not a correctness issue.
root_cause: The phrase 'at least' may imply a sufficient minimum rather than a lower bound for a first screen.
correction: Change to: 'A bounded first screen might use 200 paired examples per critical task and three repetitions per load point as a smoke test; this is not sufficient for p99 or rare-failure claims.'
acceptance_test: No reader interprets 200 examples / 3 repetitions as adequate for p99 reliability.

quoted_clause: They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.
observed: The sentence says prefix caching does not affect the decode bottleneck. But §2 explicitly says prefix reuse removes KV capacity, and Table 15-1 treats KV capacity as a binding constraint at Light and Typical load. If prefix caching frees KV capacity, it can permit larger decode batches or more concurrent decode requests, which changes decode goodput. The statement is too absolute.
evidence: §2: 'the shared prefix's KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated — removing prefill FLOPs and KV capacity'. Table 15-1: KV demand ÷ host KV budget is 0.97× at Light and 4.91× at Typical, so capacity is a first-order decode-side constraint. A mechanism that reduces KV residency can therefore affect decode, even if it does not reduce decode-time HBM traffic per active token.
root_cause: The sentence conflates 'prefix caching does not reduce decode-time HBM traffic for an active request' with 'prefix caching has no effect on the decode bottleneck'. The former is true; the latter is false when KV capacity constrains concurrency.
correction: Narrow the claim: 'Prefix caching does not reduce the decode-time HBM traffic of an already-resident request; its decode-side effect is indirect, through freed KV capacity that may permit larger batches or more concurrent requests.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer says the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching. It distinguishes direct decode-traffic effects from indirect capacity effects.

quoted_clause: recording offered load alongside p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT/ITL separately (report p95 only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s)
observed: The sentence says to report p95 only at offered loads at or below the host's admission capacity (~2 rps), but the benchmark is described as a 40 rps saturation run. It is unclear whether p95 is being recorded but not reported at 40 rps, or whether the 40 rps run is exempt from the reporting rule. The protocol is ambiguous.
evidence: The same paragraph says the 40 rps run is 'a saturation run on one host ... whose queue is expected to grow'. A growing queue means the host is above admission capacity, so the parenthetical reporting rule would exclude the very run being described.
root_cause: The sentence mixes two different benchmark goals: a saturation run to observe queue growth, and an SLO-reporting run at or below admission capacity. The reporting rule is stated without clarifying which run it applies to.
correction: Separate the two runs explicitly: 'Run A: saturation at 40 rps to observe queue growth; do not report p95 SLO numbers from this run. Run B: step through offered loads up to the host's admission capacity (~2 rps) and report p95 TTFT/TPOT only for Run B.'
acceptance_test: The benchmark protocol clearly states which runs produce reportable p95 values and which are saturation-only.

page_hint: Chapter 15, §7 What We Still Don't Know, chunked-prefill bullet
quoted_clause: real user traffic exhibits bursts (e.g. social-media events) that may require larger chunks or alternative back-pressure mechanisms
observed: The bullet says bursty traffic 'may require larger chunks'. The chapter's own chunked-prefill mechanism says smaller chunks reduce decode stall, while larger chunks improve prefill throughput but increase decode interference. For bursty traffic, the appropriate response is not obviously 'larger chunks'; it could be smaller chunks, admission control, or back-pressure. The claim is under-argued and potentially misleading.
evidence: §Two Mechanisms: 'a smaller chunk reduces the decode stall but adds scheduler overhead ... chunk size is an empirically-chosen middle'. The open question should not presuppose that bursts push toward larger chunks without stating the trade-off.
root_cause: The bullet treats 'bursty arrivals' as if they have a known directional effect on optimal chunk size, but the chapter has not established that direction.
correction: Reframe as a genuine open question: 'Bursty arrivals may change the optimal chunk size in either direction — larger chunks can drain a prefill backlog faster, while smaller chunks protect decode latency — so the chunk-size policy must be measured under the target arrival process rather than assumed.'
acceptance_test: The open question does not assert a directional recommendation ('larger chunks') without acknowledging the opposing trade-off.

page_hint: Ch 16 §3 Step 1, after FP8 KV paragraph
quoted_clause: Every TCO figure below is scaled to a named peak fleet — 21 hosts ... or 22 hosts ...
observed: The cloud default is priced on 6 hosts (4,380 host-hours), and the mini-case prices 2 hosts. The sentence's universal scope is false.
evidence: Later text: 'The canonical default bills 6 × 730 = 4,380 host-hours'; mini-case: 'two 8×H100 servers'.
root_cause: Overgeneralized scope statement; self-host Mode 1 basis was written as if it governed all modes.
correction: Restrict the sentence to Mode 1 / Table 16-1 rows A and A′, or explicitly exempt the cloud occupancy input and mini-case.
acceptance_test: Search for 'Every TCO figure below'; no unqualified universal remains, and cloud/mini-case bases are explicitly distinguished.

quoted_clause: Step 2 — price each mode on N_hosts = 21 ... with the 22-host case (ii) run priced alongside it
observed: Mode 2 is then priced on 6 hosts (4,380 host-hours), not 21; Mode 3 has no host count. 'Each mode' is contradicted by the next subsection.
evidence: Mode 2: 'The canonical default bills 6 × 730 = 4,380 host-hours'; Mode 3 is usage-based.
root_cause: Inconsistent fleet basis between the step framing and the cloud/API modes.
correction: State that Step 2 prices the self-host mode on N=21/22 and that cloud is a separate paid-occupancy input; or price cloud at 21 always-on and move the 6-host default to a clearly separate sensitivity.
acceptance_test: Step 2 and Mode 2 use the same stated host basis, or the exception is explicit in both places.

quoted_clause: ~16 GB of KV remains — 0.64 of a 9,500-token request (24.9 GB) — against 2 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 17 requests in flight.
observed: The 16 GB is per host (4 replicas × 140 GB on one 640 GB host), but 2 rps is the total across two hosts. Per host the arrival rate is 1 rps, so in-flight is ≈8.6 requests; total KV across both hosts is ≈32 GB against ≈17 requests.
evidence: Earlier: '2 rps average is 1 rps per host'; '4 replicas × 140 GB weights = 560 GB of the 640 GB pool' is a per-host calculation.
root_cause: Mixed per-host and aggregate bases in one comparison.
correction: Use either per-host: 16 GB vs 1 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 8.6 requests; or aggregate: 32 GB vs 2 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 17 requests.
acceptance_test: Recompute the KV shortfall on one stated basis; units and population match.

page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case, 'Which term is which — no double-counting'
quoted_clause: the ~$64K/month cash saving (API $104K − self-host $40K) already nets those same hours ... with the wage counted in both columns ($104K + $26K − $40K = $90.2K/mo)
observed: The $64K figure subtracts a self-host total that includes the $26K wage from an API cost that excludes the wage. The $90K figure adds the wage to the API side. These are different wage treatments and cannot both be the same cash comparison.
evidence: Table says wages are 'inside the ~$40K self-host cost'; API $104K is usage cost only.
root_cause: Inconsistent treatment of whether the 0.5 FTE engineer is paid under the API scenario.
correction: Define one basis. If the engineer is redeployed and wage is paid under API, the API-side premium is $104K + $26K − $40K = $90K. If the engineer is eliminated under API, the cash premium is $104K − $40K = $64K. Do not present both as the same saving.
acceptance_test: One wage treatment is used consistently; the $64K and $90K numbers are either reconciled or one is removed.
